output.query: exercise-triggered migraine with aura first attack differential primary exercise headache RCVS dissection

results.finding: Migraine with aura (1.2) requires at least two attacks; an attack fulfilling all but one criterion is coded probable migraine with aura (1.5.2). Primary exercise headache (4.2) is brought on by and occurs only during or after strenuous exercise; on its first occurrence subarachnoid haemorrhage, arterial dissection and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome must be excluded.
results.source: Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society. ICHD-3. Cephalalgia 2018;38:1-211

results.finding: In a clinic survey, more than a third of people with migraine reported attacks triggered by exercise.
results.source: Koppen H, van Veldhoven PLJ. Migraineurs with exercise-triggered attacks have a distinct migraine. J Headache Pain 2013;14:99

results.finding: RCVS typically presents with recurrent thunderclap headaches over one to four weeks, often triggered by exertion, sexual activity or Valsalva; segmental arterial vasoconstriction resolves within about three months.
results.source: Ducros A. Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome. Lancet Neurol 2012;11:906-917

output.summary: Exercise is a common migraine trigger. A first headache with exertion needs exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage, dissection and RCVS; RCVS classically causes recurrent thunderclap headaches.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: One attack only, so criterion A fails; visual aura meeting 5 of 6 C characteristics; confusion is an accompanying feature, not a brainstem aura; first-ever exertional attack flagged; normal examination
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache and aura history with examination and SNNOOP10 red-flag review, applying each ICHD-3 1.2 criterion
action_criteria.rationale: Migraine with aura is a clinical diagnosis made against ICHD-3. The history establishes that this is a single attack (probable migraine with aura, 1.5.2), separates the transient confusion from an aura type, and identifies the two red flags (first attack, exertional onset) that justify imaging.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal brain MRI without infarct, haemorrhage, mass or posterior FLAIR change
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI for a first-ever aura with confusion during strenuous exercise
action_criteria.rationale: A first attack with an atypical accompanying feature (confusion) and exertional onset is a red flag for a secondary cause (AHS neuroimaging evidence assessment, Evans RW et al., Headache 2020;60:318-336). MRI is preferred to CT. Recommended rather than required because the aura itself was typical and the examination is normal.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal intracranial and cervical vessels: no vasoconstriction, dissection, aneurysm or AVM
action_criteria.label: MR angiography of the head and neck for a first headache during exertion
action_criteria.rationale: ICHD-3 requires subarachnoid haemorrhage, arterial dissection and RCVS to be excluded at the first occurrence of an exertional headache; MRA covers dissection and RCVS non-invasively. Recommended rather than required because the headache followed a typical spreading aura and was not thunderclap.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Triptan, NSAID and caffeine can be combined; he has no triptan contraindication; the triptan is taken when the headache starts
action_criteria.label: Check the acute treatment plan (triptan or NSAID) against his caffeine and ibuprofen use
action_criteria.rationale: He takes no interacting drug and has no vascular contraindication, so the check does not change management.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence: ICHD-3 attack-count rule and the exclusions required for a first exertional headache
action_criteria.label: Literature on exercise-triggered migraine and the first exertional headache
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; not a clinical step in the patient's pathway.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start migraine preventive medication after a single attack.
Do not advise him to give up running: exercise is a trigger to manage, not a contraindication.
required_recommendations: Explain the diagnosis: a single attack with the features of migraine with visual aura is probable migraine with aura (ICHD-3 1.5.2); the confusion resolved with the aura and no structural or vascular cause was found, so he can return to running with graded training.

Acute plan for a further attack: stop exercising when the aura starts; at headache onset (not during the aura) take ibuprofen 400-600 mg or naproxen 500 mg, or sumatriptan 50-100 mg, with metoclopramide if nauseated.
No preventive medication after a single attack (AHS 2021 thresholds not met); keep a headache diary and review if attacks recur.

Trigger advice for training and races: maintain hydration and fuelling, keep caffeine intake steady rather than loading around races, and avoid ibuprofen during long races (kidney injury and hyponatraemia risk).
Safety-net advice: urgent assessment for a thunderclap headache, an aura lasting over 60 minutes, weakness, speech disturbance or a changed pattern.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here

accepted: Probable migraine with aura (ICHD-3 1.5.2), exercise-triggered visual aura; no structural cause

differential.key_features: Needs at least two brainstem symptoms; at most one is present (transient disorientation, with alertness preserved, if counted as a disturbance of consciousness), and there was no dysarthria, vertigo, tinnitus, hypacusis, diplopia or ataxia.
Exertional trigger, but the headache followed a spreading aura and was not thunderclap, there was a single episode, and the MRA shows no vasoconstriction.
No neck pain or Horner syndrome; normal cervical MRA.
Normotensive (112/68), no persistent encephalopathy, and no parieto-occipital FLAIR change on MRI.
Positive visual symptoms spreading over 20 minutes and followed by migrainous headache are features of aura, not of ischaemia; no vascular risk factors; no infarct on MRI.

Occipital seizures give brief, often coloured circular phenomena lasting seconds to a few minutes; a monochrome zigzag spreading over 20 minutes, no automatisms and no postictal state argue against it.

key_clinical_evidence: A single attack that fulfils the other ICHD-3 1.2 criteria is probable migraine with aura (1.5.2); 1.2.1 needs at least two attacks.
Confusion is not an ICHD-3 aura type; migraine with brainstem aura needs at least two brainstem symptoms.
A first migraine-like attack during strenuous exercise is a red flag: MRI excludes a structural cause and MRA excludes dissection and RCVS (ICHD-3 4.2 comment).
Brain MRI and head and neck MRA are normal.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The headache built up about 20 minutes after a gradually expanding visual aura and was not thunderclap; RCVS presents with recurrent thunderclap headaches, and the MRA is normal.
red_herrings.intended_effect: May anchor on RCVS or exertional subarachnoid haemorrhage

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The confusion began during a spreading hemifield visual aura and resolved with it, and he was alert and oriented when assessed at the event; a metabolic encephalopathy does not produce a spreading zigzag aura. One brainstem-type feature does not meet migraine with brainstem aura.
red_herrings.data_point: Confusion and disorientation during a half-marathon
red_herrings.intended_effect: May anchor on exercise-associated hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia or heat illness, or on a brainstem aura

sequence_constraints.reason: The structured history identifies the red flags (first attack, exertional onset, confusion) that justify imaging.

findings.result: One attack, 4 weeks ago, at about 15 km of a half-marathon. No earlier aura and no earlier significant headaches.
Visual only: flickering haze in the right peripheral field becoming a shimmering zigzag arc (positive, unilateral). No sensory, speech, motor or retinal symptoms.
Gradual expansion over about 20 min; visual symptoms resolved 30-35 min after onset.

Transient disorientation during the visual aura (did not recognise other runners, could not recall his race number), resolved with it; alert and oriented when assessed at the event. No loss of consciousness, dysarthria, vertigo, tinnitus, hypacusis, diplopia or ataxia.
Began about 20 min after the aura resolved; bilateral, throbbing, 9/10, with nausea and photophobia; built up rather than peaking instantly; lasted about 14 h.
Normal neurological examination: full visual fields, no papilloedema, no focal deficit. BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 52 (regular).

First-ever attack (new headache): present. Precipitated by strenuous exertion: present. Systemic symptoms, neoplasm history, deficit outside the aura, thunderclap onset, onset over 50, positional features, papilloedema, painful eye, trauma and medication overuse: absent.
Sister with migraine without aura; no hemiplegic migraine, epilepsy or stroke in the family.

clinical_assessment.impression: 1. A single attack fulfilling ICHD-3 1.2 criteria B, C (5 of 6) and D but not criterion A (two attacks): probable migraine with visual aura (ICHD-3 1.5.2). 2. Transient confusion accompanied the visual aura; it is not an ICHD-3 aura type, and the criteria for migraine with brainstem aura are not met. 3. Normal examination. 4. Red flags present: first-ever attack and onset during strenuous exercise.

scores.ICHD-3 1.2 criterion C characteristics m: 5 of 6 (spread, 5-60 min duration, unilateral, positive, headache within 60 min; no succession of aura symptoms)

alternatives: Naproxen 500 mg or ibuprofen 400-600 mg at headache onset
contraindications: Sumatriptan (SmPC): ischaemic heart disease, previous stroke or TIA, peripheral vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, severe hepatic impairment; not recommended in hemiplegic migraine or migraine with brainstem aura. None of these is recorded for this patient.
interactions: Sumatriptan with ibuprofen: no pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interaction; they may be taken together.
Sumatriptan with caffeine: no clinically significant interaction.
sumatriptan.proposed: sumatriptan, against current ibuprofen 400 mg as needed and caffeine 200-400 mg around training
sumatriptan.summary: No interaction between sumatriptan, ibuprofen and caffeine, and no label contraindication to a triptan in the recorded history. Sources: sumatriptan SmPC; BNF.
warnings: Triptans are taken at the onset of headache; a dose taken during the aura is ineffective.
NSAIDs taken during prolonged endurance exercise, especially with dehydration, are associated with acute kidney injury and exercise-associated hyponatraemia.
Regular high caffeine intake and abrupt caffeine withdrawal can both provoke headache.
Acute medication on 10 or more days a month (triptans) or 15 or more days (simple analgesics) risks medication-overuse headache.
Propranolol, if prevention is ever considered, lowers maximal heart rate and exercise capacity.

additional_observations: Indication: first visual aura with transient confusion during a half-marathon, 4 weeks ago.
Technique: sagittal T1, axial T2, FLAIR, DWI with ADC and SWI.
Comparison: none (outside head CT not available for review).

signal_characteristics.FLAIR: no cortical or white matter signal change

mri.impression: Normal MRI brain. No infarct, haemorrhage, mass or white matter lesion; no parieto-occipital FLAIR signal change.

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate: a single exertional attack is probable, not definite, migraine with aura; confusion is not a brainstem aura; first exertional headache needs MRI and MRA; no preventive after one attack
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Moderate: first exertional attack with confusion warrants MRI and MRA (RCVS and dissection exclusion), and the attack count limits the diagnosis to ICHD-3 1.5.2

patient.chief_complaint: Visual disturbance, confusion, and severe headache during exercise — first episode 4 weeks ago

family_history: Sister has migraine without aura; no family history of epilepsy, stroke, hemiplegic migraine, or cardiac disease

social_history.note: Sports therapist; competitive marathon runner (50-60 km/week training); non-smoker; no alcohol; high caffeine around races; no illicit drugs

patient.history_present_illness:
A 27-year-old British man was referred to the neurology outpatient clinic following an alarming episode 4 weeks ago. He was running during a half-marathon event when, at approximately the 15-kilometre mark, he noticed a flickering haze appear in his right peripheral vision that expanded over approximately 20 minutes into a typical zigzag shimmering arc. He slowed to a walk. During the aura, he also felt confused and disoriented — he didn't recognise other runners around him and couldn't recall his race number momentarily. A St John Ambulance volunteer was called. The visual aura and confusion resolved within 30-35 minutes. He was assessed briefly at the event and was found alert and oriented at that time. Approximately 20 minutes later, he developed a severe bilateral throbbing headache (9/10) with nausea and intense photophobia that lasted approximately 14 hours. He was taken to A&E where he was given IV fluids for dehydration.

He had never had a visual aura before and no prior significant headaches. He completed a head CT in A&E which was reported as normal. He is an active marathon runner (training 50-60 km/week). He is healthy, takes no regular medications apart from caffeine around training and occasional ibuprofen, has no medical history, and no family history of epilepsy. His older sister has migraines without aura. He consumes caffeine strategically around training and does not drink alcohol. He specifically denies any weakness, speech difficulty, or loss of consciousness during or after the episode. He is extremely anxious about exercising again.
